EntertainmentTab.title: Oasis live 2027: Knebworth return confirmed plus Manchester and Glasgow gigs
EntertainmentTab.text:
After weeks of posting teasers on social media and underneath the Manchester sky, Oasis have confirmed a second leg of their smash hit reunion tour for summer 2027.

The band will return to the scene of their legendary 1996 gigs at Knebworth House to play four nights at the 125,000-capacity venue in September next year.

They will also play a 11-night residency at the home of their beloved Manchester City in June, after kicking off the tour with five gigs at Glasgow's Celtic Park in May.

The announcement dropped on Monday afternoon alongside a new trailer, external and a photograph of frontmen Liam and Noel Gallagher. "Start the celebrations!", read a message on the band's social media.

"After a period of reflection, 'The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force In Recent British History' has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people.

"Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold."

Oasis will return to Slane Castle in County Meath, Ireland, for two dates in September, after performances across Europe in July and in the US in August.

Sharing the trailer on his own personal X account, Liam, 53, commented: "Spiritual."

The now confirmed 38-date tour marks the next phase of Oasis's comeback following their acclaimed 2025 live reunion, which made an estimated £300 million at the box office.

A new ticket registration process, similar to that used for Glastonbury Festival, has been launched in a bid to avoid the noise and confusion of last time around.

The registration period began on Monday with the announcement, on the band's website, and closes at 16:00 BST on Thursday 17 September.

In the UK, tickets will then go on sale across Friday 25, Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September.

The band says standard ticket prices will be fixed and range between £71.50 and £266.60.

The special guest will be Richard Ashcroft again for all dates.

Singer-songwriter Noel recently teased the band's 2027 return - after a year off - telling TalkSport, external: "There must be something happening."

The band then posted a series of cryptic videos on their official social media channels appearing to tease gigs across the UK and Europe.

This was followed by a drone display outside the Etihad Stadium last week, pointing to Monday's announcement, as well as something similar in Rome and gig posters on the Paris Metro.

Manchester City fans the Gallaghers played a string of shows together at the Etihad Stadium in 2005, almost a decade after two famous nights at their team's old ground, Maine Road, were caught on camera for a concert film titled There and Then.

A few months after Maine Road, the band played to 250,000 fans on the grounds of Knebworth House in Hertfordshire over two nights in August 1996 - shows that are regarded as Britpop's crowning moment.

More than 4% of the UK population applied for tickets to see the Gallaghers perform, alongside the likes of the Charlatans, Manic Street Preachers, The Prodigy and Chemical Brothers.

Speaking at the premiere of a Knebworth documentary film in 2021, Noel said Oasis had had "no fear" about the magnitude of the shows, adding that if they were to do it again now they would be "petrified".

The band's 2025 comeback got off to a shaky start before an E minor chord was even strummed, with fans criticising the ticket sales process after being asked to queue for hours, with some finding themselves having to pay hundreds of pounds more than they expected.

The fiasco triggered a UK government response. Following an investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Ticketmaster agreed to several voluntary changes, external, including telling fans 24 hours in advance if a tiered pricing system is in use and giving clearer information about ticket prices while people wait in the queue, as well as not using misleading ticket labels.

Demand and expectation were huge among fans, old and new. But the band delivered, with the BBC's review saying they hadn't sounded so good since the 1990s.

Mid-way through the world tour, Noel told TalkSport that he and his bandmates had been "blown away" by the response to their return after 16 years away.

Last week, another emotional documentary chronicling the tour - and featuring the reconciled brothers' first joint interview since their acrimonious split in 2009 - was released in UK cinemas, following its premiere in Venice.

In it, Noel confirms the band is "not a power struggle any more".

On Monday, following the announcement, he told the same radio station, external that booking part two of the comeback tour had been a no-brainer.

"We were having such a great time that, why wouldn't you?" said the musician, who will turn 60 on the day of the final Celtic Park concert.

He confirmed there would be no new Oasis music off the back of the tour.

Renewed interest in Oasis recently saw their second album (What's The Story) Morning Glory? officially overtake the biggest-selling album by their heroes The Beatles in the list of the UK's most popular albums of all-time.

And Wonderwall, from that album, became a bittersweet England World Cup anthem this summer.

Excitement for Knebworth has been growing for years - ever since it was rumoured to be on the itinerary for Oasis's 2025 tour.

Earlier this summer, it emerged that the band's promoters had applied for an events licence that would cover the Knebworth gigs.

Other big artists to have performed at the grounds of the listed country house venue include Led Zeppelin, Queen, Sir Paul McCartney, Metallica and, in 2022, Liam Gallagher as a solo act.

Oasis made history over two nights in 1996, but in 2003, Robbie Williams beat their combined attendance record by playing three consecutive nights, drawing a total crowd of 375,000 people.

That record now looks set to be broken again.

"This is history", as Noel once put it, now repeating itself 30 years on.

EntertainmentTab.title: Bob Mackie: Legendary costume designer dies aged 87
EntertainmentTab.text:
Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.

The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.

"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.

The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.

The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.

"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.

Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".

"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.

Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.

Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.

"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."

Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."

"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."

Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.

He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.

EntertainmentTab.title: Diljit Dosanjh: Punjabi singer makes history under the famous Wembley arch
EntertainmentTab.text:
On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"

Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived".

But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase.

Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said.

Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said.

And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from Born to Shine to Lover.

Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran.

He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet".

His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star.

Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him.

In London, Dosanjh's crowd was largely - but not entirely - South Asian.

The hype for his appearance was building all afternoon, with fans arriving early to get in place.

"MJ [Michael Jackson] and Madonna, he's that level for us," said one fan. "He's so good looking, and so down to earth," said another.

"Diljit. I love you more than my husband," declared a third.

When he came on the stage shortly after 8pm, dressed in traditional attire, the stadium erupted and the screams barely stopped for the next two-and-a-bit hours.

His soulful voice echoed around the stadium, demonstrating his range, as he blended homegrown Punjabi music with rap and hip-hop.

Throughout the show, the audience waved lights, sang along and - of course - danced.

At times, the standing area closest to the stage resembled an Indian wedding, with fans copying Dosanjh's energetic moves.

But despite performing in such a vast venue, Dosanjh proved again his ability to connect on a personal level with fans.

He brought fans on stage, giving them gifts and taking selfies, and also shouted out those in the back rows of the 90,000-seater stadium, saying they were "full of heart".

There was also exciting news for fans in India, as he announced he would be performing in November at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad.

The concert was capped off with the emotion of the night - his track Main Hoon Punjab, which means "I am Punjab" - set to a spectacular firework display.

"What an incredible show, the energy and vibe was unparalleled!" concert goers Amit and Rani told the BBC.

They added that it was not only a privilege "but a moment to celebrate for Punjabi culture".

Dosanjh likes a "first".

From humble beginnings as a small village boy from Punjab, he made history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi-language singer to perform at the US music festival Coachella.

He also famously made his Met Gala debut decked in majestic Punjabi attire.

His meteoric rise has seen him perform across America and Europe, and collaborate with pop stars from Sia to Sheeran.

His authenticity is a big part of his appeal. He remains true to his Punjabi roots, wears his turban as a sign of pride, and sings in his mother tongue.

Away from music, Dosanjh is also a popular Bollywood actor - and a social media sensation. Even those who haven't heard his music have probably viewed his funny Instagram videos - such as him arguing with an Amazon Alexa device, external that couldn't understand his accent.

Now, he's performed on a stage that's previously been home to titans of music from Taylor Swift to Coldplay.

For Dosanjh and his millions of global fans, it means Punjabi music, Punjabi culture and Punjabi vibrancy has reached an historic moment.

Speaking to the BBC before his gig, he said he felt "thankful" to be here.

"When we were going to book this venue, everyone said, 'Think again before you book, it's a big stadium'," he said.

"I said: 'We'll see whatever comes. I want that our people are happy and can say yes, we can do this too!'"

He reflected on the many artists who had performed there before him, adding that to follow their footsteps "means a lot, a lot".

"It may not mean as much for someone like Harry Styles, as much as it means for us. He has performed on such stages, but for us, it's very special. Coming from a village to here - it's very special."

"I feel good. I feel happy. And I feel good for my people. I feel good for the next generation," he said.

And of course, there was only one way he could end.

"We are here. Punjabi Aa Gaye Oye!"

EntertainmentTab.title: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'risky' comeback show in Paris
EntertainmentTab.text:
Iconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.

The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring.

Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.

Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at Paris' La Plenitude Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena.

"I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.

"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.

"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.

She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."

"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."

They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.

Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.

The Mirror's Lucy Needham, external noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".

"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."

After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".

The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.

She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."

She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.

"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."

Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.

She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."

Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.

Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".

She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.

"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.

The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.

"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., external

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."

The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.

"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024.

"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."

When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.

The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.

Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.

Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.

Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.

Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.

Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.

And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Forget Notting Hill - we set our new romcom in the east end of Glasgow'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Film fans have had plenty of chances to spot Glasgow on the big screen in recent years, from superhero blockbusters to futuristic sci-fi thrillers.

Now the city is to star in cinemas once again - but the difference is that it won't be doubling for another location. It is actually set in the city.

Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget that is the fraction of Hollywood productions like Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The indie film - by writer and director Kevin Walls - was shot across the city, meaning landmarks such as Kelvingrove Art Gallery pop up - a well as the less obvious location of an east end flat.

The film stars James Rottger and Elle Watson as Cameron and Eilidh - mismatched flatmates who face the prospect of parenthood after a one-night stand.

"We shot quite a bit in a flat in the east end, maybe about nine days there," Walls said.

"There is a key scene we did in a close there. It is not necessarily the most romantic location you would think of for a romcom, but in real life that's exactly where these things happen.

"Why can't we set a romcom in a flat in the east end? It looks really beautiful on the big screen."

That vibe is something the film's leading lady agrees with, despite Glasgow's film appearances often being due to it looking Gothic.

"We are so used to Glasgow being this dark and gritty place, but that's not reflective of the city overall", Watson said.

"It's great having it on screen as a bright and funny place, with people falling in love there. Shooting in locations I've grown up around was great too, as I've been going to Kelvingrove since I was a little kid.

"Part of me wanted to run around the building when it was all quiet. But when you see it on the screen it looks beautiful. Being from Glasgow you are so used to it that you almost become immune to the spectacle of the building, and how grand it is."

Walls admitted to BBC Scotland News that some of the choices were made through necessity.

"The locations were tricky because we didn't have any money," she said. "So we were begging – I'd usually go down and speak to people about what I was trying to do. I explained I wasn't going to tear up their space or anything like that."

Premature is the first feature film Kevin has directed, having worked on short films and adverts in the past.

He has also juggled other jobs, including lecturing and editing highlights of football matches for YouTube channels, with money raised going back into Premature.

A Kickstarter campaign helped secure funding needed for a cinema release.

"Cinema-going is really important to me, and through sheer determination I was going to get this on a cinema screen too, as it deserves to be seen there", Walls said.

Watson's character Eilidh harbours dreams of being an artist, but is frustrated that life is not going to plan. Her flatmate Cameron is meticulous and career driven, but everything changes for both of them when they drunkenly sleep together.

"This whole film is about two people being chucked out of any sense of control they thought they had," said James Rottger, who plays the leading man.

"Particularly for Cameron, that's the point of the film – I leaned into the bit of me that's a control freak and likes to do things a certain way, and then brought that out in the character."

Like his co-star, he was delighted to see so much of Glasgow on screen, and being presented in a bright light.

"It's brilliant big productions are coming here and using Glasgow as a double, but it's important we see Scotland on the big screen as itself," he said.

"The film Kevin has written shows Glasgow in a warm light, literally and figuratively. The red sandstone flats, Kelvingrove, the pubs – it's all there."

For Watson, the relatability came in a different way.

"Any woman in her late 20s or 30s will have thought about children, it's omnipresent," she said.

"You feel you need to be confident about your choice as it will soon be taken away from you as you get older.

"But it was important the film is not just about Eilidh being pregnant – it's using that for her to discover who she is and what she wants from life."

Walls admits he had to overcome his own doubts during the creative process, having put so much effort in.

"There were so many times you'd think 'what am I doing here, this is a terrible idea and won't work' – I had to push past that and be confident," he said.

Seeing the finished product in cinemas will make it all worth it though, as Watson sums up.

"It feels like a miracle for this film with a tiny budget and a hope and a prayer, to be on the big screen."

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Bear with me here, but I’m beginning to suspect Sydney Sweeney is a very fine actor. It’s a skill she has been recognised for in the past, of course, winning nominations for Emmys for Euphoria and The White Lotus, but I mean it in a deeper sense, related to her work in advertising rather than drama – can she do more than play a role? Can she make you feel what she’s feeling?

In her “controversial” new ad for the sports prediction site Novig (the scare quotes are because, when you’re begging for controversy this hard, you shouldn’t just be handed it on a plate), she adopts the garb of various sports. Her face, body, aspect, gait and mien are all carefully configured to amp up the erotic overtones to the maximum degree, and yet the feeling that beams out of each image is: “This is really going to piss people off, and I couldn’t be more delighted.” Her expression is so speechful that you cannot help but share in some of her hellion joy.

In brief: the proposition of the betting site is that it’s only for betting on sports – no wars, no deaths, no politics, just sports. Even the captions, absent the Sweeney, are a red rag to a bull, since betting on wars and death is a disgusting and inhumane thing to do – the surge in people trying to spin cash out of deaths in Iran, in Ukraine, says something profound about where we’ve got to in late capitalism. Whatever that profound thing is, it’s definitely not funny.

However, we are where we are, and that’s not Sweeney’s concern. She is there to wrinkle out the double entendre from every conceivable crevice. Do spherical things remind you of breasts? What if I get these two American footballs and put them in front of my actual breasts? Would it help if I was naked to the waist? Ah, better still if I were wearing no clothes at all and only the footballs stood between me and my modesty? The age-old tennis shot, immortalised by the 80s Athena poster in which the viewer is invited to consider just how nearly they can see a player’s butt – well, that’s here, only this time minus the skirt.

Sweeney’s facial expressions are like a WikiHow gallery, “how to: soft-porn” – they often feel quite old-fashioned, pert or faux naive, more like 70s graphic novel erotica than modern, up-to-the-minute pornography. Yet, throughout, there is a layer of knowingness: “I know exactly how much I’m going to drive you mad, and why.”

Truthfully, it’s hard (as a card-carrying member of the wokerati, just out here in the world, trying to keep up) to figure out what the fundamental provocation is. Sweeney famously last made headlines with the “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” ad for American Eagle Outfitters. It was taken by many to be a call back to Donald Trump’s “You have great genes, you know that?” speech, which itself was taken as a densely layered challenge to the world, that his supporters were better human specimens than everyone else. Was the speech white supremacist or simply Trumpian-supremacist? You couldn’t really stick anything on him because, as ever, it was only atmospherically decipherable. Sweeney, however – with her very blondness, her unarguable whiteness – people did stick a white-supremacist agenda on, one she soon decried, saying she was against “divisiveness”.

Ever since, Sweeney has been taken as an anti-woke poster-girl, though since nobody can agree what “woke” means, still less what “anti-” it entails, this poster is more confusing than an avant garde typographer’s ball. She seems to want to kick that hornet’s nest with this Novig ad, but is it by inviting her own objectification? Or is there a complicated message in there about femaleness in elite sport, which has become such a lightning rod for anti-trans activism? Or are we supposed to disapprove of the pornification of the visual realm?

None of the above! Ariarne Titmus, four-time Olympic gold medal-winning swimmer, explained on Instagram: it’s “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”. And now she says it, yes, that makes perfect sense. What Sydney Sweeney’s game is, beyond almost-naked tennis, is anyone’s guess.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent
EntertainmentTab.text:
Neil Marshall, writer/director

I was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well … caves. At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, “OK, everybody, turn your lights off” and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn’t fathom.

We wanted the film to feel as realistic as possible: when you’re caving, the only lights you have are what you take with you. There are no beautiful shafts of light making everything look pretty. It meant having huge portions of the screen in total darkness, so only when a character turns around and shines a light you finally see what’s in the shadows.

Darkness was definitely my friend, but it did mean a lot of planning because each character had to have something they could light the scene with, even if it was just a box of matches. Sam McCurdy, the director of photography, and I discussed lighting sources that we could potentially use, and I structured the film around who had which light at which time. This gave us a lighting scheme: if you’re with the fire, it’s Sarah. If it’s a torch, it’s Juno.

There isn’t a single real cave in the whole film. It was a mixture of amazing sets by Simon Bowles, a couple of matte paintings and a miniature set built by Leigh Took – the water pouring down the waterfall wasn’t water, it’s salt.

For the crawlers, I wanted something very basic-looking, not too many lines or details. The challenge was how to make them scary but keep them human, because the notion is that these are the cavemen who stayed in the cave rather than those who left the dark and started building cabins in the open. Visually they were a hybrid of Nosferatu and Iggy Pop, but movement-wise I thought we should make them like spiders – the way they’ll stop and be perfectly still before suddenly going off at 100 miles an hour and then stopping again.

I conceptualised the film as Sarah’s descent into being this primal savage: her undergoing a rebirth in order to survive, even though you’re not sure she’s going to be able to go back to society afterwards.

Shauna Macdonald, played Sarah

This was the era of FHM, Loaded and all those lads’ mags, so I initially thought it was going to be girls looking sexy in tight spaces covered in blood and gunge. I wasn’t interested in that. When I read the script, though, it was excellent. It was about a grieving mother and I also needed to be physically strong and brave. I thought, “I have to do this part because I don’t know if I’ll be able to pull it off.”

We weren’t allowed to see the crawlers or even any pictures of them. I was the first to see one because we were shooting chronologically once we got into the caves. The others were all asking “what does it look like?!” but I didn’t really know because it was quite far away. I just knew it was grey or white and slimy, and it looked a bit like Gollum.

I think Neil was right to keep us apart, because when we were faced with them, I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked, who’d been training for months and months – that really focuses the mind. When we came to fight them, they were so animalistic it was really unnerving. The actors had figured out how the crawlers’ system worked and their different characteristics. You felt like you were fighting a pack with all its dynamics, and that was pretty intimidating.

That whole sequence where Sarah goes into survival mode was great. First I had the dying scene with Alex Reid, who played Beth, just making it look really easy. It was like, “OK, Alex, you’ve had an ice pick through your neck, but it’s really important that you tell these plot points …” And she was, “Yeah, cool, no problem.” And then, of course, I cave her head in with a stone. Then I get leapt on by a child crawler. He was only like 11, bless him, and I crushed his head with my boot, which was actually me stamping on a cauliflower. Then the mother finds out, and we have this fight sequence where one mother has to kill another to survive. The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying. Then another crawler comes along and I bash his head in too. Afterwards I’m submerged in this pool of blood, which was a Jacuzzi that they’d overflowed. This amazing stunt girl had to do the run and jump, because the pool was so shallow they couldn’t insure an actor to do it. All I had to do was emerge and take the glory.

In the press, it was all about “girl power”. But we were like: “Have you seen what we do to each other?!” What was very girl power was how fiercely we actors supported each other and we continue to do that. The only way you can really show love is by turning up for your friends, and the six of us have done that repeatedly for the last 21 years or so. We’ve got a WhatsApp group and still meet regularly. I do wonder, if we’d met on a different project, would the same thing happen? Or was it the film? If you throw a group of people in a cave, maybe you all come out bonded for life.

EntertainmentTab.title: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts
EntertainmentTab.text:
Oasis have finally confirmed new tour dates for 2027, including their long-rumoured return to Knebworth for a run of shows 30 years after they played a historic two nights at the Hertfordshire venue in 1996.

“Start the celebrations!”, the band said in a statement. “After a period of reflection, The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force in Recent British History” – a quote from a Guardian opinion piece about the band – “has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people. Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold.”

Titled Oasis Live 27, the dates encompass the UK, Ireland, mainland Europe and the US, beginning in Glasgow on 21 May, and touring through Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston, Las Vegas and Slane Castle (north of Dublin), ending with four nights at Knebworth in September.

The band had teased the news in a massive drone display above Manchester’s Etihad stadium last week, after hinting at the dates on Instagram.

The tour follows Oasis’s acclaimed 2025 reunion, which saw them play 41 dates spanning the UK, Europe, North and South America, east Asia and Australia, 16 years after they split in 2009. “You struggle to think of another artist that’s received such a vociferous reception,” wrote Guardian critic Alexis Petridis in a five-star review of the first night of the tour in Cardiff.

The 2027 tour will be Oasis’s first visit to mainland Europe since their reunion and adds US cities they didn’t visit during that run. Their return to Paris will be particularly poignant, given it was shortly before a 2009 set at the city’s Rock en Seine festival that the band first split up.

In the UK, tickets will cost between £71.50 and £266.60. Those hoping to buy them will have a happier experience than those in the same position last year: all pricing information for Oasis Live 27 has been shared in advance after action by the competition watchdog forced Ticketmaster to change how it advertises tickets, including ending “misleading” information about seats, after fan backlash over its handling of the 2025 tour.

Last year, the use of “tiered” pricing meant that some fans, expecting to pay £148.50 per ticket, found themselves faced with costs of £350 at the checkout – and only a matter of minutes in which to decide whether to go ahead with their purchases. Now, Ticketmaster must tell fans 24 hours in advance if tiered pricing will be used, which tickets it covers and how the system works. When the sale is live, the price range must be shared and updated as tickets sell out.

Anyone wanting a ticket for 2027’s tour must register between now and 4pm BST on 17 September. The registration has been introduced “to reduce queuing times and organised ticket touting in order to give genuine fans the best possible chance to buy tickets,” according to organisers.

Fans had a chance to revisit the 2025 tour – or catch up on what they missed – as a documentary about the reunion, Don’t Look Back in Anger, hit cinemas last week after premiering at the Venice film festival. It earned glowing reviews for its emotional portrait of the band’s fans.

The documentary didn’t touch on the furore around ticket prices, other than one onstage comment from Liam Gallagher: after referring to the people in the cheap seats, he added: “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.”

The news that Oasis would return to Knebworth was first teased by an unlikely suspect, the British peer Baroness Taylor of Stevenage. In October 2025, she suggested in the House of Lords that Oasis would be playing five shows “in the fantastic venue of Knebworth House”, just a mile away from her own residence.

She quickly retracted her comments in the chamber, clarifying to the Guardian that she was “speaking hypothetically following speculation that they would play Knebworth again as they did in August 1996”.

In August, it was reported that SJM Concerts managing director Simon Moran had secured an events licence for Knebworth, prompting further speculation about an Oasis appearance. The licence would cover audiences of 125,000 people.

At the original 1996 dates, the band played to 250,000 fans – just one tenth of the number who applied for tickets, estimated at the time to be more than 4% of the entire British population. “This is history,” Noel Gallagher told the Knebworth crowd on the second night. The band recently started selling replicas of Noel and Liam’s respective outfits on the night.

A 2021 documentary, the prosaically titled Oasis Knebworth 1996, positioned the concerts as “the peak of British culture” wrote Guardian music editor Ben Beaumont-Thomas in a four-star review. The film’s voiceovers, he continued, implied that “all live music went downhill afterwards. It’s a lie every generation tells itself.” Liam subsequently headlined the park in June 2022.

UK Music estimated that the band’s five nights at Manchester’s Heaton Park last year led to music tourist spending in the north-west rising 16% year on year to £1.4bn. Momentum behind the tour was also credited with boosting the UK’s ongoing vinyl revival.

Oasis are also rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027, the festival’s return after a fallow year in 2026.

Their reunion poured more fuel on the fire of enduring Britpop nostalgia, sparking a critically panned play documenting the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, an album called Britpop by Robbie Williams and even an embrace of Oasis in the US, a country that had been historically immune to their charms.

Celtic Park, Glasgow: 21, 23, 25, 28, 29 May

Etihad Stadium, Manchester: 4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, 22, 25, 26 June

Allianz Arena, Munich: 2, 3 July

EntertainmentTab.title: The desecration of DC: from a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocity
EntertainmentTab.text:
When you have a developer as US president, you might expect some zhooshing up of the capital. A few buildings renovated, maybe some parks replanted. But when you have a megalomaniac builder in charge, things can get out of hand. A decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected, I asked what it might mean for the US to be led by a real estate tycoon whose career had left a trail of broken promises, angry buyers and endless lawsuits, with rules flouted, heritage trampled and the world pockmarked by a fleet of aspirational towers clad with a flimsy veneer of luxury. The answer is worse than I could have imagined.

With the air of a nightmarish Hollywood sequel, Trump 2 has seen the president’s true architectural ambitions unleashed: The Blingpire Strikes Back. As America’s self-styled decorator-in-chief, Trump has not only overseen the gilded mutilation of the White House, but embarked on the Mar-a-Lagofication of Washington DC itself, applying his gold paintbrush to statuary, daubing ponds with flaking pool liner, and brewing plans for a colossal triumphal arch – all procured in a blizzard of no-bid contracts. And, in true dodgy salesman style, this programme of bauble-building is turning out to be a high-profile decoy for deeper damage being wrought elsewhere.

The bloated White House ballroom is the most emblematic project of Trump’s reign so far, a chandelier-bedecked warehouse conceived on a scale that would make Ceaușescu blush. Standing like an overly iced wedding cake atop a multilevel concrete bunker, it is a swaggering confection that masks deep-rooted paranoia: a decadently wrapped panic room, where a besieged dictator might hole themselves up.

“It won’t interfere with the current building,” Trump promised last July, when he announced the plans. “Not touching it.” It would seat 650 guests and cost $200m, funded by private donations. Less than three months later, without waiting for congressional approval, he tore down the historic East Wing, and dumped the rubble on a nearby public golf course (which he also plans to redevelop). The ballroom ballooned, as if injected with rapid weight-gain formula, to seat 1,000 in a building three times the volume of the White House. The price has also tripled to $600m, at least half of which will now be picked up by the taxpayer.

Trump boasted that his ballroom will be “more beautiful” than Versailles, but it looks like something thrown together from the classical off-cuts bin, without any regard to how the pieces fit. “It has all the kneejerk gestures of classicism,” a former Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) official told me, “but they are not integrated in a way that makes any sense.”

A sweeping ceremonial staircase leads to nowhere. A grand pedimented entrance is shunted to one end of the east facade. The portico columns run four rows deep (“The supreme court is three deep,” Trump noted. “No other building has it, and I did it because it’s incredible.”) The ballroom’s proportions are so out of whack, it will make the White House look like a lopsided fiddler crab, the swollen appendage vastly dwarfing the original building.

The inflated scale was too much to bear for its architect, the bowtie-wearing James McCrery II, who protested at the increasingly Frankenstein nature of the classical details being applied. Enter Shalom Baranes, whose DC firm has handled multibillion dollar federal contracts, including the renovation of the Pentagon after the 9/11 attacks.

Baranes’s experience with fortified facilities has come in handy, given that the project has evolved into what Trump now calls “the Magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex”. The party hall, the president confirmed in March, “essentially becomes a shed for what’s being built under” – namely a six-storey military-grade bunker, replete with a command and emergency operations centre, a full-scale military hospital, secure telecommunications hubs and situation rooms, all serviced by specialised air-handling and filtration networks to protect against biological, chemical and radiological threats. “It’s meant for if there’s a nuclear attack,” Trump has boasted. “The concrete is so hard, I’m not sure you could take it down.”

Behind the overblown cornice, the ballroom’s roof will be home to a military drone port and air-defence missile system. Images show it looking like an aircraft carrier parked next to the White House. In typically Trumpian newspeak, the project has gone from being a space to entertain dignitaries to a “desperately needed National Security structure” that must be completed at all costs.

After court rulings halted construction, the supreme court recently weighed in to allow it to resume – although, tellingly, the ruling made no comment on the project’s legality. But questions in the courts have revealed just how far Trump’s aides see his absolutist rule extending. “If the government decides, very quickly, to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty,” one judge asked, “nothing can be done?” A lawyer for the administration responded: “I think that’s right, yes.”

Similarly bullish efforts are being made to force through the president’s second flagship vanity project, the elephantine triumphal arch. It was casually announced last October, with 3D-printed models displayed like tacky souvenirs in the Oval Office. It is planned to tower 250ft above Memorial Circle, a vast roundabout on Columbia Island in DC’s Potomac River – 1ft for every year of US independence. But there has been no ambiguity about what the looming edifice is really there to honour. When asked, Trump simply replied: “Me.”

It “will be the GREATEST and MOST BEAUTIFUL Triumphal Arch,” he boasted on social media, “anywhere in the World”. He has cited Roman precedents and “the one in Paris”, adding that his version “will surpass it in every way”. Oddly, given his fondness for the North Korean regime, he has neglected to mention Pyongyang’s Arch of Triumph, built in 1982 to mark Kim Il Sung’s 70th birthday. Clad with 25,500 blocks of sparkling white granite, one for each day of Kim’s life, its crowning stone slab rises 10m taller than Trump’s (although his is topped with a statue for an extra 25m of vanity height). Hitler’s Triumphbogen, also unmentioned, would have been twice the size.

To aid his Napoleonic cosplay, the president has hired Harrison Design, purveyors of gaudy McMansions from Atlanta to LA, with the arch project led by Nicolas Charbonneau, principal of the firm’s Sacred Architecture Studio. Charbonneau first sketched the idea to illustrate an April 2025 essay by conservative critic Catesby Leigh, titled Washington Needs an Arch. It proposed a modest structure of 60ft. Trump got hold of the idea and, with his irrepressible lust for supersizing, pumped it up fourfold.

As with the ballroom-bunker, the arch has become larger and more encrusted with gilded ornament – in a word, more Trumpian – as it has progressed. The final design, unveiled this April, features a 60ft golden-winged Lady Liberty sprouting from its summit like an oversized cake-topper, flanked by two plump eagles. Even Trump’s allies have suggested the design could be toned down. At a CFA review, McCrery, the first ballroom architect, advised removing four golden lions from the base of the arch. “They’re noble, they’re courageous, and they’re strong,” he noted. But “they’re not of this continent”. The arch must celebrate American triumphs only – and that goes for the animals too.

The National Park Service has determined the project will “adversely affect” dozens of historic sites around DC, while a group of Vietnam veterans has filed a lawsuit, arguing the arch will be an unwelcome “expression of domination”, with its observation deck looming over Arlington National Cemetery. Neither of these are proving to be obstacles, with excavation set to begin soon.

Preliminary works do not augur well. A mockup of the arch was erected for the Great American State Fair in July, made of plywood wrapped with white vinyl. It buckled in the heat, its surfaces warping and peeling, while globules of expanding foam oozed from its wonky cornice. It was instantly dubbed the Temu arch – a fitting moniker, given that Trump’s Oval Office swags appear to have been sourced from the fellow Chinese online marketplace Alibaba.

The ballroom and the arch received tens of thousands of objections from the public, but both projects were fast-tracked through the system. As the former CFA official told me, it was “highly unusual” that the initial concept schemes were granted final approval without details being resolved. The ballroom took just 12 minutes of deliberation. And it has set the tone of things to come. There’s nothing a developer hates more than red tape, and Trump has vowed to streamline regulations across the board. Beyond speeding up his DC follies, the proposed changes will lubricate drilling, pipe-laying and datacentre building, in the name of “reclaiming America’s proud heritage as a nation of builders”.

Obscured by all the controversy around these trophy projects is the fact that the administration has moved to weaken protections on historic buildings and landscapes drastically, unleashing the steamroller of development across the country. The changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act would narrow the definition of historic places, exclude consideration of the “visual, atmospheric or audible” consequences of projects on historic sites, and reduce requirements for consulting Indigenous tribes and the public. As Brent Leggs, president of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, remarked, it would “eviscerate the preservation of our shared civic and cultural heritage in the United States”.

The irony couldn’t be clearer. Trump bloviates about continuing America’s tradition of monument building, while weakening the very mechanisms that exist to protect the country’s heritage. Still, by slashing these protections, at least he is paving the way for his own additions to be toppled just as hastily as they were erected.

Given the construction quality so far, future topplers might not need much help. The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has now been drained for a second time, after the coating used in the first $15m renovation began peeling off within days of its completion. Despite a new filtration system intended to keep the water a pristine shade of “American Flag Blue”, massive algae blooms quickly turned it a swampy green. While Trump blamed vandals, justice department legal filings eventually conceded the failure was due to the “hasty and botched” renovation. “I have a guy who’s unbelievable at doing swimming pools,” Trump boasted, before awarding the no-bid contract to a company that had worked on his Virginia golf course.

Elsewhere around the capital, the “Safe and Beautiful” initiative has seen $76m spent on fountains, $5m on gilding a pair of equestrian statues of The Arts of War and The Arts of Peace, $500,000 on a single statue pedestal to display a statue of a prominent slave owner, which had been removed from Delaware amid Black Lives Matter protests, and countless other acts of cosmetic surgery in the name of cleaning up the “cesspool” of DC.

One of the crowning trinkets will be the National Garden of American Heroes, for which $40m has been ringfenced. According to Executive Order 13978, this park of 250 statues will “reflect the awesome splendour of our country’s timeless exceptionalism” in the face of the “reckless attempt to erase our heroes, values and entire way of life”. The list of figures to be commemorated includes slave owners and others whose statues were toppled in the wake of George Floyd’s murder. Sculpture experts described the proposed timeline as “completely unworkable” and likely to produce “slapdash and uninspired” work, suggesting the only place with foundries capable of realising a project on this scale and speed would be China. Alibaba prepare!

Trump’s construction mania is all-consuming. He uses press conferences to show off his latest renovations and has spoken of how building is the “fun” thing he does to relax, in between kidnapping South American presidents, bombing the Middle East and bullying Greenland. But White House insiders say his therapeutic hobby has become the policy priority, a massive drain on the administration’s energies and resources.

The Resolute desk has never seen so many samples and swatches – whether marble for the Lincoln bathroom, golden drapes for the East Room, or the “million-year lifespan” pavers for the driveway – a White House shopping list that now tops $900m. The Oval Office looks like a developer’s showroom, most recently displaying a two-metre model of Trump’s $22bn makeover of Dulles airport, boasting gold-mirrored ceilings and “the largest garage in the world”.

The closer autocrats come to their end, the more frenziedly do they build. Nero embarked on a golden palace before he was driven to suicide. Marie Antoinette built a model hamlet before she was beheaded. Hitler pored over architectural plans in his bunker during his final days. Trump is buried in catalogues of fixtures and fittings, busy inspecting the workmanship of his helipad-cum-cocktail patio, as the country crumbles around him.

EntertainmentTab.title: Touring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital support
EntertainmentTab.text:
When Radiohead started touring, it was hugely exciting, but we got signed when we had been going for five or six years and had only really played in Oxford. Suddenly you’re entering a new world: the first flush of fame, being compared to everyone else, the furnace-like experience when a band takes off and a whole new routine of late nights, bad food and everything else that goes on around live music. Everything is heightened and it can be very isolating.

In 1992 we were playing small venues in a van and then suddenly in 1993 we were spending the second half of the year in the US. On our second long tour that year, everything caught up with me. I kind of withdrew into myself. Something about being in the US made me feel “impostor syndrome”. I really did feel a very long way from home. All that anxiety has to come out somewhere – for some it’s drink and drugs – but for me it came out in my playing. There was one particular show where we were opening for Tears for Fears and another band who had [Blondie’s] Clem Burke on drums. Clem was my absolute drummer hero but I just hit peak overwhelm, and my drumming went off a cliff. Every limb seemed to be going at its own speed. The kick drum became like trying to open a heavy door.

By the end of the tour it was very noticeable. I was lucky in that I could speak to my wife – this was pre-Zoom or FaceTime, so meant very expensive phone calls! – but after that tour one of our managers asked me to go and have a chat and broached it with me very nicely. Having that space to begin talking about it was absolutely invaluable. Similarly, when we opened for James and then REM, they became kind of mentors: seeing how other people navigate it all was fascinating.

On Radiohead’s tour last autumn, with the help of the Music Industry Therapist Collective, we were able to put an initiative in place to support the health and well-being of all tour personnel. The MITC provided introductory sessions during rehearsals and production build, and confidential drop-in therapy sessions were available to anyone in the touring party during the tour if they wanted them. But until now there’s been nothing like that available for bands playing venues like the ones we did when we started.

At that level, your margins are nonexistent, your workload is much greater – loading the gear and so on – and you’re driving yourself between shows. You’re expected to get your head down and get on with it, but it can mean times when you’re not necessarily looking after yourself physically and you can feel very isolated. There’s an emotional and geographical displacement in moving from place to place and living on top of each other. There’s the sound check, the gig, meeting people afterwards, anxiety that some people guiding you may not have your best interests at heart. You can feel really vulnerable, and there’s no way of getting off that roundabout until you get home. It’s difficult to talk about because nobody wants to rock the boat, and other people might be going through the same thing, so you don’t want to burden them.

That’s why I’m supporting a new project called the Pay It Forward Fund, which has been set up by Tamsin Embleton and the Music Industry Therapist Collective to provide much-needed mental health support for musicians and crews on smaller tours, having grown out of the kind of help MITC already provides to larger tours. If someone is looking to reach out to a therapist, it can be really good to talk to someone who has lived experience in the music industry, so this project will mean people have someone to talk to who understands what they’re going through. I’ve volunteered for the Samaritans since I was a student and know how important it is to talk.

I’d have really appreciated something like the Pay It Forward Fund back in Radiohead’s early days, so that’s the kind of space I hope it can provide. Initially £272,000 is being provided to finance 150 tour teams of practitioners over a three-year period, an occupational health, mental health education and pastoral care programme for crews and artists on smaller tours. Hopefully after that it will become an everyday part of touring and make the sort of difference it would have done for me. You might be on the other side of the world, but you can reach out and talk to somebody face to face.

Applications for the Pay It Forward Fund are now open. MITC’s book Touring and Mental Health: the Music Industry Manual, edited by Tamsin Embleton, is published by Omnibus

EntertainmentTab.title: Beck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase
EntertainmentTab.text:
The last time Beck released an album it was 2019 and the singer-songwriter found himself in a strange and unenviable position. In some quarters, the arrival of Hyperspace was eagerly anticipated precisely because his personal life was in turmoil. Nine months before its release, his 15-year marriage to actor Marissa Ribisi had ended in divorce, an experience he understandably described as heartbreaking. Unfortunately for him, there exists a pervasive argument that Beck’s greatest work is born out of misery.

His beloved 2002 album Sea Change featured a set of disconsolate acoustic songs written in the wake of a break-up with his long-term girlfriend Leigh Limon that Beck had initially thought were too personal for public consumption. They were certainly very different from the knowing, postmodern approach with which he’d made his name, but no matter: Sea Change went on to become a huge critical and commercial success. It wasn’t entirely clear what prompted the gloomy mood of 2014’s Morning Phase, but it very much seemed to be cut from similar musical and lyrical cloth. Some critics suggested it was the best album of his career; it subsequently won three Grammys, including album of the year. Given the circumstances, there was much pre-release speculation that Hyperspace would be a companion piece.

Instead, Hyperspace was synth-heavy, produced by Pharrell Williams and clearly influenced by vaporwave: its tone was dreamily buoyant and noticeably light on wracked soul-bearing. After its release, Beck seemed to tacitly suggest to fans of Sea Change and Morning Phase that there wouldn’t be any more where they came from. “When I try to shoe-horn my life into a song,” he told the New Yorker, “it gets really ham-fisted.”

Seven years on, he appears to have reconsidered. The first thing you hear on Ride Lonesome is a softly strummed acoustic guitar, echoey pedal steel and Beck’s voice. “Walk away, hang your head on the hollow moon,” he sings, as the album’s title track gets under way: should there be any lingering doubt about the mood it’s intent on evoking, it goes on to reference Julie London’s Cry Me a River and Johnny Thunders’ You Can’t Put Your Arms Around a Memory. “It feels like I’ve been here before,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him.

He certainly has. There’s an intentionality about the way Ride Lonesome reconvenes the team responsible for Sea Change and Morning Phase – the former’s producer Nigel Godrich is once more behind the mixing desk, the backing musicians who appear on both albums are present and correct, the orchestrations are the work of Beck’s father David Campbell – and about the artists the music here evokes. As on Sea Change’s Round the Bend and Morning Phase’s Heart Is a Drum, the ghosts of Nick Drake and his string arranger Robert Kirby are very clearly summoned up, most noticeably on In the Night. On Run Away, we find Beck exactly where he was on Sea Change’s The Golden Age and Morning Phase’s Unforgiven: alone, behind the wheel of a car in the small hours, aimlessly driving around in an attempt to assuage his unhappiness.

Similar sound, similar mood, similar lyrical themes: of course, the danger is of diminishing returns. But Ride Lonesome never feels like a pale imitation or a craven attempt to recapture past glories. That’s partly because of the standard of the songwriting. Beck has suggested that one reason the album took so long to make is because of stringent quality control: songs were recorded, then set aside for years, then reconsidered, a huge amount of material was discarded. You can tell: everything here, from the sparse country-rock of Slow Canyon to the lush, harmony-drenched Falling Through My Hands is melodically exquisite; every song has the requisite emotional impact.

But it’s also because Ride Lonesome is clearly an album made by a noticeably older artist than either of its predecessors: its mood is marked not just by the collapse of a relationship, but a sense of time passing, of things – to borrow a phrase from Nick Drake – moving just a little too fast. “I don’t know where I’m going,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him, “but it feels like I’ve been here before”: a neat capturing of a very mid-50s kind of malaise. An affecting sense of weariness seeps into everything, even the ostensibly optimistic – and utterly lovely – closer Beyond the Light comes filled with evocations of lost “nameless days” and of “the dying of the light”.

Unfortunately for Beck, Ride Lonesome does little to dispel the aforementioned theory about his best work being born out of unhappiness. There’ll be consolation in the fact it’s also that rarest of things: a sequel to a sequel that’s every bit as good as its predecessors.

GeneralTab.title: Lucy Letby: Thirlwall inquiry report into nurse's crimes due to be published
GeneralTab.text:
The findings from a public inquiry into how Lucy Letby was able to repeatedly murder and harm babies will be published later on Tuesday.

The Thirlwall Inquiry was set up to look into what happened at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 2015 and 2016, while Letby was working as a nurse in the neonatal unit.

Letby, now 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice.

The inquiry was not tasked with examining Letby's guilt. Instead, it investigated how concerns about the neonatal nurse were handled by the hospital and whether action could have been taken sooner to stop her.

Among the key questions the report may answer is whether any babies might have lived or avoided injury if action had been taken earlier.

Letby was moved from the neonatal unit to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team. But the inquiry has been examining whether alarm bells should have started ringing earlier, for example in June 2015 after three babies died in quick succession.

The inquiry, led by one of the country's most senior judges Lady Justice Thirlwall, involved six months of evidence and thousands of documents at a cost of more than £18.5m.

It is expected that the report will find there were significant safeguarding failures, and will recommend changes across the NHS.

The chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC would be paying close attention to the report.

Letby has previously been denied permission to appeal against her convictions on two occasions.

Her defence lawyer Mark McDonald told BBC Newsnight on Monday he had submitted "nearly 30 expert reports to the CCRC really undermining the whole safety of the convictions" - and that it was "more evidence" than "any other case" in the CCRC's history.

He added: "If she is innocent, as I believe, as 30-odd experts believe, then everything that has gone before the inquiry and every recommendation has operated on the wrong premise."

GeneralTab.title: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
GeneralTab.text:
The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

It is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published,, external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons, external that cap would be £100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK. Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.

Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address? Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?

The Communities Minister Baroness Taylor told the Lords that Brits returning from abroad and wanting to donate without limit "must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom" and the government is "considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy".

In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.

Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.

Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?

The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.

Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.

GeneralTab.title: Nato jets shoot down drone that flew into Lithuanian airspace
GeneralTab.text:
Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.

Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."

The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.

Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.

Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.

Nausėda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Moscow has not commented on the incident.

Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.

Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".

These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.

Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.

Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

GeneralTab.title: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
GeneralTab.text:
When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning".

"I was absolutely living paycheque to paycheque. Every time the smallest thing came up, it was like 'Oh, gosh, the kids need shoes, how am I going to afford that?' As a single parent, everything falls on my shoulders."

Last year, Brianna left Portland and its metropolitan population of 2.5 million people.

She and her two children moved 2,000 miles east to Muncie, Indiana, a small city with 65,000 people, a university and lots of open space, taking advantage of a scheme that contributed $5,000 towards the cost of the move to boost population growth.

The relocation has been a revelation for her finances. She continues to work remotely for the same bank, so her annual salary of $107,000 (£79,000) is unchanged, but she has been able to buy a home for the first time. And her mortgage is less than she used to have to pay in rent.

In Portland she was paying rent of $1,290 a month for an apartment, while the combined cost of her mortgage, home insurance and property tax for her detached home in Muncie is $1,100.

Add the fact that state income tax is lower in Indiana, and that her car insurance and energy bills have also fallen, and Brianna says she is $600 a month better off.

"I'm able to live my life more than I was before," she says. "When my kids want something, I'm much more inclined to say yes. My quality of life has increased dramatically."

Brianna is not alone in swapping a big city for a smaller one.

As the high cost of living continues to bite in the US, many of the biggest cities are seeing their populations fall, as people leave in search of cheaper property.

A 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors found that for people moving to a different state, affordability was their primary reason., external

As a result, big cities from the likes of New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Oregon have seen a dip in their populations, external in recent years, further fuelled by the greatly increased acceptance of remote working since the Covid-19 pandemic.

By contrast, some small towns and cities across the US, such as Muncie, are seeing their populations rise after decades of decline. The number of people who live in Muncie hit 65,466 last year, official figures showed., external This is up from 65,194 in 2020, but still way down on its population of 71,828 in 1990.

To help it stand out from the crowd, and encourage remote workers to move there from outside Indiana, Muncie's local council offers them $5,000 in cash to cover their relocation costs.

It does this via a website called MakeMyMove, which lists several such relocation support schemes offered by similar small cities and towns across the US. These pay MakeMyMove a subscription fee.

Other incentives locations offer potential new residents are complementary cinema tickets, restaurant vouchers, and even free bottles of wine.

Brianna and her children are one of around 100 families to have moved to Muncie through the MakeMyMove programme. She says she hadn't heard of the city before.

Across the US, MakeMyMove says it helped 1,000 people in total relocate last year, and is on target to increase that to 1,500 in 2026.

Scientist Elena Chrysostomou also used a relocation support scheme to swap a big city for smalltown US. In 2024 she relocated from San Diego, California, to Jacksonville, a town of 17,700 people in rural Illinois.

The move was backed by the Jacksonville Regional Economic Development Corporation (JREDC), which gave her $5,000 in cash, plus a "quality of life package" worth $4,000 that includes free gym memberships and golf passes.

The JREDC says that while the region is "already a great place to live", the support scheme helps to "sweeten the deal".

Elena was spending $3,000 renting a one-bedroom apartment in San Diego, but she now owns a three-bedroom home, with a mortgage of $1,868. At the same time, her salary has gone up 22% after she changed jobs, and her commute has gone down from a 15-minute drive to one of just one minute.

"I never thought that I'd be able to afford a house on my own, I always thought I'd need a partner, and even then, in San Diego, it would be so tough," she says.

"It's just more freeing. There's more security and independence."

While both she and Brianna have no regrets, they do admit to some drawbacks to their new lives. These include the narrower range of activities and restaurant choices, leaving behind friends and family, and for Brianna the difficulty of settling her children into new schools.

And while in Portland Brianna enjoyed walking to parks and shops, she now relies on her car to get anywhere.

But overall she says she is thrilled. "I have the biggest savings I've ever had in my life, and I'm a homeowner, and I can do things with my kids – we actually went on vacation for the first time in my youngest's life."
